transcript.text: I run an online shop in the UAE. I believe our revenue fell in the first quarter of 2026 against the last quarter of 2025, and my manager wants me to build a machine learning model that predicts revenue. I am the analyst; the result goes to the head of sales, who decides where to spend the next quarter's marketing money. The table I shared is our order export: one row per order, with its date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer. I do not know why revenue fell, or whether the export is complete for the latest months. [shares sales.csv]

I read your brief as two questions: is the fall real and how complete is the data, and where should the next quarter's marketing money go. Here's what the export itself says.

You're right about the drop. Gross revenue went from 101,379.97 in Q4 2025 to 84,653.28 in Q1 2026 (433 orders down to 378, average order value 240.81 down to 231.29). Paid-only revenue fell too: 87,551.17 to 72,682.06. Refunds rose from 9.2% of orders to 11.1%, while cancellations eased slightly, 5.1% to 4.8%.

The fall is not spread evenly. The app channel dropped from 40,026.95 to 27,423.51, while web only slipped 44,412.09 to 40,371.17 and store was flat at 16,940.93 versus 16,858.60 — the app alone carries most of the loss. By region: Dubai 40,730.82 to 33,882.27, Abu Dhabi 24,783.32 to 21,318.59, Ajman 11,578.89 to 7,764, Ras Al Khaimah 7,249.16 to 5,177.75, Sharjah barely moved at 17,037.78 against 16,510.67.

On completeness: your orders run 2025-01-01 to 2026-03-31, and March 2026 has 120 orders (26,122.16) against 127 in March 2025, so the last month isn't obviously truncated. I can't prove the export is complete without your source system, so I'm treating it as a working assumption.

My approach: diagnose first, then forecast. The plan — 1) break the drop down by channel, region and category, gross and paid-only; 2) separate volume from price and refund leakage; 3) check whether one segment or one month drives it; 4) only then build a revenue model on the segments that survived scrutiny, validated on held-out months. Three ways to start, pick one:

choices.title: Find which segments lost the most (drop decomposition)
choices.what: Ask the export quarter by quarter and break the fall from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 down by channel, region and product category, both gross and paid-only, plus refund and cancellation rates per segment, so we see which segments lost volume, which lost order value, and which lost money to refunds. You get: A ranked list of the segments that lost the most revenue, and a clear read on whether the drop is demand (fewer orders) or quality (more refunds, smaller baskets) - which is what the head of sales needs before choosing where to spend. Trade-off: It explains the past quarter; it does not predict the next one. Effort: Fast: a handful of queries on the table you already shared.

choices.title: A revenue monitor the head of sales can keep using
choices.what: Build a small dashboard that stays in this chat and can be refreshed: quarterly and monthly revenue with the paid-only line, orders, average order value, revenue by channel and by region for the two quarters side by side, and refund and cancellation shares over time. You get: One page the head of sales can read in a meeting, and the same numbers re-run when next quarter's orders land. Trade-off: Monitoring, not diagnosis: it shows the split but does not chase the cause through each segment. Effort: Quick to set up from the same table.

choices.title: The revenue prediction model your manager asked for
choices.what: Train a forecasting model on monthly revenue per region and channel: target that month's paid revenue, inputs date, month number, segment, order counts, average basket, refund rate and past revenue, validated on the last months held out rather than on random rows. You get: A revenue number for the coming quarter by segment, and a sense of how wrong it is likely to be - useful as a planning baseline for the marketing budget. Trade-off: It can forecast a level, but with no ad-spend column it cannot tell you which channel gives the best return on a dirham spent; and the amount and status of the same order cannot be inputs, or they leak the answer. Effort: Longest: a project with a holdout and metrics, and honest error bounds.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a travel agency. I want to predict, at the moment a booking is made, whether it will be cancelled, so the operations team can overbook the right trips. The table I shared is our bookings up to late February 2026: booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Some of the trips in it have not happened yet. Operations would score every new booking once, on the day it is made. [shares bookings.csv]

Here's what I read from your brief and from the table itself.

**The problem underneath.** You need a per-booking cancellation probability that is honest *at booking time* — which means two things your data tests right now: only fields known that day, and labels that have finished playing out. Of your 1,500 bookings, **318 have a travel date after the February cut**, so a "not cancelled" flag on those just means "not cancelled yet". Training on them as negatives would teach the model that future trips rarely cancel. I'd fit on the **1,176 closed bookings (22.1% cancelled)** and keep the open ones out of both training and scoring. Two other things I noticed: `free_cancellation` barely moves the odds (22.6% vs 23.3%), so the signal lives elsewhere; and `price` is stored as text, so it needs coercing before it can be used at all.

**Plan**, once you pick:
1. Freeze the label window — closed bookings only, and say so in the report.
2. Keep booking-day features only (`booking_date`, `travel_date`/`lead_time_days`, `destination`, `nationality`, `channel`, `price`, `free_cancellation`); drop `booking_id` and `customer_id`.
3. Split by time, not at random: train on earlier bookings, test on the most recent (Nov 2025 – Feb 2026, about 408 bookings) — that mirrors how operations will actually score.
4. Judge it against the 22.1% base rate, and check calibration, since overbooking needs a believable probability, not just a good ranking.
5. Hand back the riskiest segments so operations can sanity-check the model against what they see.

Three ways in, above — the model is the one I'd start with, and the rule profile is a useful thing to compare it against.

You get: A probability per new booking, plus how it beats the 22.1% base rate on the untouched recent window, and which segments (destination, lead time, channel, nationality) carry the most cancellable bookings. Trade-off: The 318 bookings whose trip has not happened yet are set aside, so roughly 1,176 rows train the model; seasonality beyond this window is not tested. 5. **Score what's left open.** The 318 future-trip bookings come back with a cancellation probability each — that's the shape of the daily job.

I'll report the risky segments too, so operations can sanity-check the model against what they already see.

Say the word and I'll run it.
